There is a gradation here with some games falling on different parts of the random-procedural spectrum, but ultimately every instance of procedural generation is "controlled randomization." One game is pretty poor at this, being more random than procedural in my books, but another is actually incredibly clever and inventive in how it sews its levels together. From a design point of view, it has a ton of interesting lessons.

Lots of traditional roguelikes, including early examples and classic titles, have little in the way of interesting procedural generation. Rooms and corridors are laid out randomly, as are items and monsters. There is no part of the game concentrating on making interesting levels; it just mashes things together with a few constraints and hopes for the best. Which actually works great! It makes things unpredictable and leads to bizarre and memorable situations. But if you want real procedural content creation, check out something with graph-based level planning.

In most of my games, non-player characters (NPCs) have specific patterns rather than complex artificial intelligences (AIs). Often this means approaching the player and performing a special action every x turns, or approaching the player but with an individual movement pattern. With a variety of different units around, it's easy for this to quickly become an interesting system for the player. It's all deterministic, so players can predict ahead of time and plan moves instead of having to second guess complex AI algorithms.

The one roguelike I didn't implement this in just has random AI movement, some with slightly different weightings depending on the unit's characteristics. I've seen interesting discussions from players on how the AI is super-smart and tries to keep in safe areas. It's all false, but humans are great pattern spotters. This taught me that there's no point in spending time on complex AI - humans don't notice it well and will imagine that simple AI is complex anyway.

Some behaviors that work quite well:

- Maintaining a certain distance range. For ranged attack monsters, summoners, or support units, give it a minimum and maximum distance to stay from the player and actions to perform while in that range. This is intuitive for the player to understand and suitably challenging to overcome.

- Pack tactics. A unit stays a minimum distance from the player unless there are multiple units within a certain radius of the player. This leads to very clever-feeling units that will stick close to the player and then all pounce in together. Works best in open area maps.

- Hit and run pack. This can be a bit tricky, but it's effective. Enemies stay ranged, and once they have a minimum number in their group, they charge in. Once they make an attack, they switch back to ranged. Combine it with strictly ranged healing enemies for added fun.

- Multiplying next to the player. Sounds simple, but it's quite effective. Traditional units split when away from you or when hit. Restrict it instead to multiplying only when next to the player and only multiplying into adjacent spaces, and it can be a threatening unit that can still be carefully managed.

- Stealth enemies that are invisible except when adjacent. This leads to fun when you know an enemy is near and you want to just corner it so you can be next to it and hit it easily.

For AI pathing, I like to use a scent map (add scent-1 to each player-adjacent tile, and scent-(range) to each adjacent to that, etc.). This lets me give modifiers to terrain to encourage certain behaviors more, like avoiding walls (or sticking to walls if I want). In one of my games, I did this and had the scent slowly fade, which meant that standing in an area for a while would create a scent hotspot that enemies would gravitate to instead of chasing you. This helped as part of the whole laying traps gameplay.
